The early life history of the Mud sole Austroglossus pectoralis begins with the release of pelagic eggs during the spawning season. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from the chorion at an extremely small size, with the wet weight at birth calculated to be approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of a related flatfish species. These yolk-sac larvae remain entirely lecithotrophic for a brief period, absorbing their endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The transition to active feeding marks a critical juncture where mortality rates are highest, as larvae must successfully detect and capture suitable planktonic prey to sustain further growth and development. Following this trophic switch, the pelagic larval phase progresses through a series of morphological changes including flexion and the onset of fin ray ossification. The entire pre-metamorphic period is strongly influenced by ambient water temperature, and field data suggest that optimal developmental conditions occur at approximately 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], which promotes efficient yolk utilization and rapid somatic growth during the early larval stages.

As the pelagic larvae grow, they undergo a pronounced larval metamorphosis involving a dramatic body plan reorganisation, including the migration of one eye to the opposite side of the head and the assumption of a benthic lifestyle. This habitat transition from a planktonic existence to a demersal one is accompanied by significant allometric shifts in body proportions. Upon successful settlement, the post-metamorphic juveniles occupy sandy or muddy substrates in nearshore environments, where they begin feeding on small infaunal invertebrates. Growth during the juvenile stage is relatively rapid, and individuals attain a total length at puberty of 33 centimeters [Lp = 33 centimeters] upon reaching sexual maturity. This size marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, after which individuals are considered reproductively viable. In terms of body mass at this developmental milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 214.4 grams [Wwp = 214.4 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for this species.

The reproductive biology of sexually mature adult Mud sole is characterised by an iteroparous strategy, with spawning occurring over an extended period during the austral spring and summer. Gravid females release their gametes during broadcast spawning events, with individual fecundity being a function of body size. At the optimal thermal regime of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], females produce approximately 82 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 82 eggs per day] over the course of the spawning season, leading to a total annual reproductive output that can be substantial. This daily fecundity rate reflects the maximum reproductive capacity of the species under favourable environmental conditions, though actual realised fecundity in the wild may be lower due to food limitation or other ecological constraints. The protracted spawning period ensures that at least a portion of the larval cohort encounters favourable planktonic conditions, thereby buffering against interannual variability in prey availability. Spawning adults are typically found in aggregations over sandy bottoms at depths ranging from 20 to 100 meters.

Females of Austroglossus pectoralis can attain considerable sizes, with the ultimate total length for females recorded at 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters]. This maximum size is achieved after several years of sustained growth, during which individuals allocate resources primarily to somatic development before shifting investment toward reproduction. The corresponding ultimate wet weight at this asymptotic length is approximately 1330 grams [Wwi = approximately 1330 grams], based on the species-specific length-mass allometry. Such a large body size places this flatfish among the larger members of the family Soleidae in southern African waters. The growth trajectory from the 0.00018 gram [Wwb = 0.00018 gram] hatchling to the 1330 gram adult represents an increase in mass of over seven orders of magnitude. This remarkable growth potential is supported by a diet consisting primarily of polychaete worms, small bivalves, and crustaceans, which are abundant in the soft-bottom habitats the species occupies throughout its benthic life.

This age estimate was derived from otolith-based ageing studies conducted on individuals sampled from commercial trawl catches along the South African coast, and it reflects the oldest individuals observed under the prevailing thermal conditions of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C]. The combination of a 13-year maximum lifespan (13 years) [am = 13 years] and a relatively late onset of sexual maturation at 33 centimeters [Lp = 33 centimeters] total length suggests that this species employs a conservative reproductive strategy, investing heavily in somatic growth and survival over many years before and during the reproductive phase at a temperature of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C]. Natural mortality in older individuals is primarily attributed to senescence and the gradual breakdown of physiological homeostasis, though predation by larger piscivorous fish and marine mammals also contributes to overall mortality rates in the population.
